title: Ushasta: "the self within all — show me" — "you cannot see the seer of seeing" (3.4)
hook: a challenger some identify with a famine survivor from the Chandogya demands to be shown the self the way you'd point at a cow
tomorrow: Kahola: the self beyond hunger and thirst

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhujyu's question from a spirit, and the razor-thin gap at the edge of everything; vayu, the wind, carried the Parikshitas through. Your line was beyond the world.

A man starving in a famine eats leftover beans from an elephant driver to stay alive. Then the driver offers him water, and he turns it down: water, he says, I can find anywhere. That's Ushasti Chakrayana, in the Chandogya we read last month. Some readers take him to be today's challenger, Ushasta Chakrayana. Whoever he is, he's practical. He doesn't want theory. He wants to be shown. Point to it, he says, the way you'd point to a cow.
screen: `A MAN WHO SURVIVED ON LEFTOVER BEANS.` → `NO THEORY.` → `POINT TO IT.`

segments.voice: Yajnavalkya, he says, explain to me the Brahman that is right here, direct, not secondhand: the self that is within everything. That is your self, Yajnavalkya answers, within everything. Which one, Ushasta asks, is within everything? The one that breathes in with your in-breath and out with your out-breath. That is your self, within all. Ushasta isn't having it. You've explained it the way someone says, that's a cow, that's a horse. I asked for the direct one. And here Yajnavalkya gives the answer this day is named for: na drishter drashtaram pashyeh. You cannot see the seer of seeing. You cannot hear the hearer of hearing. You cannot think the thinker of thinking. You cannot know the knower of knowing. That is your self, within all. Everything else is sorrow. And Ushasta falls silent. Here's why the cow won't work. Everything you can point to is something seen. The self isn't something seen. It's what's doing the seeing. Your eye sees the whole room and never once sees itself. A flashlight lights up the path, and the one thing it can't shine on is its own bulb. Yajnavalkya isn't dodging the question. Ushasta asked for it to be shown, and the one thing that can never be shown is the one looking. For Yajnavalkya, that doesn't make it far away. It makes it nearer than anything you could point to.
screen: `SHOW ME THE SELF WITHIN ALL.` · `NOT LIKE POINTING AT A COW.` · `YOU CANNOT SEE THE SEER OF SEEING.` · `THE EYE NEVER SEES ITSELF.` · then, large: `THE SEER.`

segments.voice: With your eyes open and soft, notice what you see, then gently try to turn around and find the one who's seeing; you won't find it as a thing. Close your eyes and do the same with sounds: hear, and then look for the hearer. Don't strain; rest in not finding it, and in the seeing still going on.
Ushasta. The man who wanted the self pointed out like a cow, and heard about the drashta, the seer, who can never be seen, because it is the one looking.
Your line: the seer. Tomorrow, the same question asked again, word for word. Day three hundred seventy-five, done.

howItsDone: Teachers of Advaita Vedanta use this passage in self-inquiry, inviting students to turn attention back toward the one who sees; commentators of several Vedanta schools discuss the line about the seer of seeing.

fork.setup: Ushasta says: don't describe it. point to the self within all, the way you'd point to a cow. you're Yajnavalkya. what do you say?
options: you cannot see the seer of seeing.
fork.reveal: you cannot see the seer of seeing. the self can't be pointed to, because it's the one doing the looking. Ushasta falls silent.

original.note: Sanskrit draṣṭṛ (nominative draṣṭā): the seer, from dṛś, to see.

trapdoor: what you thought: Yajnavalkya dodged the question.
what it means: the self can't be shown, because it isn't something seen. it's the seeing itself.
what a scholar hears: na dṛṣṭer draṣṭāraṃ paśyeḥ (3.4.2). the Chandogya's Ushasti Chakrayana (1.10–11) is identified by some readers with this Ushasta.

chat.says: If the self is real, why can't anyone just point to it?
options: Because it's the one doing the seeing; you can't see the seer of seeing.
Because it's hidden far away in heaven, too distant for anyone to see.
Because only Yajnavalkya had seen it, and he refused to share it.
chat.meaning: Yajnavalkya says you cannot see the seer of seeing: everything you point to is seen, and the self is the one doing the seeing.

Ushasta.meaning: the fourth challenger, who wanted the self pointed out

Brahman.meaning: the ultimate reality, the ground of everything

na drishter drashtaram pashyeh.meaning: you cannot see the seer of seeing

Yajnavalkya.meaning: the sage answering every challenger in Janaka's court

notes: Ushasta (BU) and Ushasti (CU) Chakrayana: often identified, but not certain; the script says 'scholars often take him to be'. Confirm.

Chandogya 1.10: Ushasti eats kulmasha (beans/grain) left by an elephant driver (ibhya) and refuses the water as leftover. Confirm details ('last month' refers to the Chandogya block, days 332–359, though day 334 or nearby may not have told this story).
'Everything else is sorrow' renders ato 'nyad ārtam; confirm.
Sanskrit transliterated without diacritics: na dṛṣṭer draṣṭāraṃ paśyeḥ.
